I am 62 years old and have farmed in Quzhou County for over forty years. I finished high school, so unlike many of my neighbors, I read the county agricultural extension bulletins carefully and follow the technicians' advice on improved varieties and input timing. My household has 8 mu of flat, irrigated land. At my age I do not want the back-breaking hand labor that cotton or vegetables require, and I do not want to take risks with unfamiliar crops. The wheat–maize rotation is the only system that gives me a steady grain income and can be managed almost entirely with machinery.

My winter wheat—an improved variety called Jimai 22—was sown last October after rotary tillage. It is already in the ground, and now that the growing season is starting I will manage it through to harvest in early June. I will irrigate four times: green-up water, jointing, heading, and grain-filling. I topdress urea at the jointing stage. I keep a close eye on aphids and powdery mildew, so I will spray insecticide twice and apply herbicide once. I expect about 1 000 jin per mu, which is roughly 500 kg.

As soon as the wheat is harvested, I will plant hybrid maize—Denghai 605, a variety I have trusted for several years. I will not till the soil between crops; no-tillage direct seeding into the wheat stubble saves diesel, preserves soil moisture, and lets me plant quickly during the narrow sowing window. The maize will get two irrigations and the same pesticide schedule: two insecticide applications for corn borer and aphids, plus one herbicide. I expect about 1 100 jin per mu, or 550 kg.
